 2       II.      FINDINGS AND RECOMMENDATIONS


 3   Q   Please summarize your findings.

 4   A   My primary findings are:

 5             1. Company witness Jennifer Nelson has proposed an excessive return on equity of

 6                10.7%, well above the current authorized ROE (9.0%), the 2025 national average

 7                for electric utility authorized ROEs (9.84%), and the cost of equity of the U.S. stock

 8                market as calculated by me later in my testimony (9.87%).

 9             2. The Company’s calculation of the Equity Risk Premium is flawed, as it assumes

10                unsustainably high long-term growth rates.

11             3. The Company inappropriately uses only short-term earnings projections as the

12                perpetual growth rate in the Discounted Cash Flow model.

13             4. The Company inappropriately uses adjusted betas in its Capital Asset Pricing

14                Model analysis that do not account for regulated utilities’ lower systematic risk.

15             5. The Company uses the circular Bond Yield Risk Premium method, which anchors

16                the risk premium to previously authorized ROEs that are themselves excessive, and

17                has been rejected by FERC for being redundant and circular.

18             6. The Company’s proposed equity ratio is also excessive and would unjustly increase

19                costs to ratepayers.


20   Q   Please summarize your recommendations.

21   A   Based on my findings, the following recommendations are in the public interest:

 8             III.      COST OF CAPITAL - PRINCIPLES


 9   Q         Please explain the concept of cost of capital and its significance.

10   A         The cost of capital is the return demanded by investors on the capital they supply to the

11             Company.1 It is the weighted average of the costs of the various classes of capital supplied

12             by investors — in this case, debt and equity. The cost of debt and cost of equity are each

13             weighted by the respective amounts of debt and equity in the Company’s total capital

14             structure, so the equity/debt ratio is another important component of the cost of capital.

15             The cost of debt can be easily determined from the interest rates lenders demand on debt

16             issued by the Company. The cost of equity, however, is the product of market expectations

17             that can only be estimated by examining a number of factors.


18   Q         What is the cost of equity and how is it differentiated from ROE?

19   A         The cost of equity is the opportunity cost faced by equity investors. It is the minimum

20             return that an investor would accept to provide equity to a company. The cost of equity is


     1

 1             a theoretical concept and cannot be precisely observed. It can only be estimated through

 2             widely-accepted financial methods that gauge how the market rates the risk of an

 3             investment. The ROE, by contrast, is the actual return that the company earns on its

 4             investments. It is an accounting concept that can be directly observed through company

 5             financial statements, and can be higher or lower than the actual cost of raising equity in

 6             the market.


 7   Q         Should the Commission aim to authorize an ROE in line with the utility’s cost of
 8             equity?

 9   A         Yes. As I will explain, the public interest is served by an ROEthat is authorized to be as

10             close to the actual cost of raising equity in the market as possible. Estimating the cost of

11             equity for a regulated utility must be done carefully so as to arrive at a return that ensures

12             rates that are “just and reasonable,” a principle elaborated on in the landmark U.S. Supreme

13             Court cases that set the legal standards governing public utility regulation, Bluefield Water

14             Works & Improvement Co. v. Public Service Commission of West Virginia, 262 U.S. 679

15             (1923) and Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591 (1944).

16             In Hope, the Court found that the “just and reasonable” standard implies that first, “the

17             return to the equity owner should be commensurate with returns on investments in other

18             enterprises having corresponding risks.” 2 This concept is essentially the same as the cost

19             of equity. The opportunity cost of a particular company’s equity is determined by “returns

20             on investments in other enterprises having corresponding risks” because those are the

21             returns an investor is losing the opportunity to receive by instead investing in a particular

 1             company. Therefore, one criterion for a “just and reasonable” ROE for a utility is that it

 2             equals the utility’s actual cost of raising equity in the market.


 3   Q         What other criteria are there for a “just and reasonable” return?

 4   A         In Hope, the Court also found that the return should be “sufficient to assure confidence in

 5             the financial integrity of the enterprise, so as to maintain its credit and to attract capital.”3

 6             But the Court was also clear that determination of a “just and reasonable” return also

 7             requires consideration of the interests of the company’s customers. “The fixing of 'just and

 8             reasonable' rates… involves a balancing of the investor and the consumer interests,” the

 9             majority opinion in Hope stated. 4 Indeed, just as a return for a utility that is set below the

10             amount “commensurate with returns on investments in other enterprises having

11             corresponding risks” causes the utility to lose wealth relative to what it would earn with a

12             more appropriate return, a return that is set above this amount will cause the utility’s

13             customers to be overcharged and lose wealth relative to what they would be charged using

14             a lower and more appropriate return, and thus, would not serve the public interest. In this

15             latter case, that wealth is instead transferred from customers to the utility holding

16             company’s shareholders.


17   Q         What methods may be employed to determine the cost of capital?

18   A         In Hope, the Supreme Court explained that it is the result reached, not the method

19             employed, which is controlling, and that result should be a rate that people would

 6   A        No. A higher return implies higher risk, so approving ROEs that are higher than market

 1   Q   If regulated utilities are less risky than the market, then why have regulated utilities
 2       historically been awarded ROEs above market returns?

 3   A   Given that regulated utilities tend to be less risky than the market as a whole, the most

 4       likely explanation for higher returns is that public regulatory commissions have tended to

 5       accept estimates for ROE that are above the cost of equity.


 6   Q   What factors have contributed to commissions approving ROEs that exceed the cost
 7       of equity?

 8   A   Determining the cost of equity is inherently an exercise in estimation, which invariably

 9       includes some degree of subjectivity. Subjective factors can influence any human decision-

10       making process, including the decisions of public utility regulatory commissions, leading

11       to unintended results. These factors include the influence of utilities in the regulatory

12       process. Utilities often have more resources to advocate for higher ROEs and amplify their

13       position more effectively than opposing groups, regardless of whether their arguments are

14       stronger. This imbalance can skew regulatory outcomes and undermine the public interest.

 About this report
This quarterly report presents a comprehensive analysis of electric and gas rate case
decisions issued in the US during 2025, along with select aggregated historical data.
The report uses data included in RRA’s rate case database, available on S&P Capital IQ
Pro. RRA tracks all “major” rate cases for investor-owned utilities nationwide, defining
“major” as cases where the utility is seeking a rate change of at least $5 million, or
where the commission approves a rate change of at least $3 million. Beyond base
rate cases, the database includes details on certain limited-issue rider proceedings,
particularly those involving significant rate base additions outside of a general rate
case. Certain rate cases included in the database may not conform to the rate change
coverage criteria, to provide continuity of coverage for a given utility.

Historical data in this report may differ from previous reports due to variations in
presentation, such as the treatment of withdrawn or dismissed cases and the inclusion
of cases not previously included in RRA’s coverage. In addition, in early 2026, RRA
enhanced its dataset of rate case decisions to include decisions rendered as part of
formula-rate plans that were previously not fully reflected in the averages as well as
decisions authorized each quarter in Pennsylvania for the utilities distribution system
improvement charges as part of the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission’s quarterly
earnings review process. The enhanced dataset is still in the process of being backfilled
for the years prior to 2020. Accordingly, this report presents the legacy RRA-based
dataset and the enhanced dataset, which reflects improved granularity, particularly
regarding authorized returns on equity. However, it is currently only backfilled for the
period 2020 through 2025. Because the process of backfilling historical observations is
ongoing, the enhanced dataset is not yet complete for all years.




The Take
In 2025, the average authorized return on equity for US electric utilities increased modestly versus 2024, while
average authorized ROEs for gas utilities were essentially flat.

The modest upward movement occurred alongside a higher interest rate environment, but ROE adjustments
have not been proportional to interest-rate changes. Regulators have become more cautious about raising
allowed ROEs as customer affordability concerns intensify, especially given inflationary cost pressures, elevated
wholesale power costs and rising bills tied to accelerating capital investment (grid modernization, resilience, and
policy-driven build-out). At the same time, regulators face heightened political pressure to manage customer rate
increases as accelerating capital investment has spurred an active rate case agenda and creates incremental
upward momentum in customer bills.

While the overall averages increased or remained flat, ROEs set in general rate cases for both electric and gas
utilities in 2025 edged slightly lower than 2024, indicating that rate case outcomes were more constrained than
the broader all-authorizations average, which reflects return determinations in limited-issue rider proceedings.

RRA anticipates this surge in rate case activity will continue, as elevated interest and inflation rates and the need
for significant capital expenditures show no signs of abating. Moreover, additional expansion is expected to come

 Interest rates — as measured by the 30-year US Treasury bond yield — declined
steadily from 1990 to 2020, exerting downward pressure on authorized ROEs. During
this period, Treasury yields dropped by over 700 basis points, from 8.61% to 1.56%.
Meanwhile, the average authorized ROEs for electric and gas utilities combined
decreased by less than 325 basis points, from 12.69% to 9.56%. Notably, average
authorized ROEs for all cases did not fall below 10% until 2011 for gas utilities and 2014
for electric utilities. The calendar-year averages fell below 9.50% for the first time in
2020 for the electric group.

The overall decline in authorized ROEs coincided with an increase in rate case activity.

Between 1990 and 2020, interest rates and authorized ROEs declined at different rates,
leading to a widening spread between authorized ROEs and the average yield on 30-
year US Treasurys. This spread increased from just over 400 basis points in 1990 to
about 800 basis points in 2020.

The widening spread is primarily due to regulators’ implicit understanding that the
interest rate drop driven by US Federal Reserve intervention was atypical. Consequently,
regulators did not fully reflect the interest rate drop in newly authorized ROEs. In some
instances, regulators recognized that industry changes and economic instability posed
increased risks for investors, justifying a higher premium over interest rates.

The spread has been narrowing since 2020 — when interest rates began to rise, but
authorized ROEs did not keep pace — reaching about 500 basis points in 2025. Given
the various factors increasing customer bills and increased affordability scrutiny, the
spread may continue to narrow, as regulators may become more reluctant to raise
authorized returns.


Capital structure trends
The negative cash flow impact from the 2017 federal tax legislation raised concerns
regarding utility liquidity and credit metrics. In response, many utilities sought higher
common equity ratios. Consequently, the authorized equity ratios adopted by utility
commissions in 2019 averaged 49.94% for electric utilities and 51.86% for gas utilities,
modestly higher than the averages for 2018 and 2017, and almost 300 basis points
above the levels observed in 2005.

RRA has noted significant differences in average ROEs based on the types of

Due to the restructuring of the electric industry, several states have unbundled electric

have jurisdiction only over return parameters and revenue requirements for distribution
operations.

RRA finds that the annual average authorized ROEs in vertically integrated cases
involving generation assets have historically been about 30-67 basis points higher
than in distribution-only cases. This difference is attributable to the increased risk
associated with the construction, ownership and operation of generation assets, as
well as the procurement of fuel supplies.
